$comment: What a trace frame's `detail` carries, per kind — the half of the Code Server wire that the version gate could not see.

R-50: `detail["loop"]` was added to the runner and the release number was not moved. The netcrawl-sdk 1.4.1 on PyPI and the deployed UI both reported 1.4.1 and disagreed about the frame shape, so `isSupportedSdkVersion` compared equal and admitted a runtime that emits no loop identity. `indexLoops` skips any frame whose `detail.loop` is not a number, and the stage draws the track only when that index found an instance — so the whole feature, its 「迴圈」 header included, was simply absent. Nothing failed; the player read it as unbuilt.

RUNTIME_PROTOCOL_VERSION does not cover this. It gates the shape of commands the server sends *to* a runtime; a frame is what a runtime reports back, and the two move for different reasons. This file is what covers it: `sinceVersion` names the first release that emits the shape below, and the server's MIN_PYTHON_SDK_VERSION may not sit under it. That is the link that forces the floor, which forces the starter workspace's lock, which cannot be locked at a release that was never published.

Three tests read this file, and a shape change has to answer all three: the runner in this tree emits exactly these keys (packages/sdk-python/tests/test_frame_contract.py), the *installed* runner does too (scripts/test-python-sdk-artifact-lifecycle.py — in the steady state that is the artifact on PyPI, which is the assertion R-50 needed), and the UI reads no key that is not declared here (scripts/test-frame-contract.mjs).

R-259 adds value.detail.references as required semantic evidence: Name loads that actually executed, with exact source spans. It distinguishes `a = b` from identifier-looking text in `a = "b"` and executed branches from short-circuited or unselected branches; without that evidence the UI degrades to static state instead of guessing.

`required` means every frame of that kind carries the key. Anything conditional belongs in `optional`, and the conditions are easy to miss: `taken` is absent on an `assert`, which has a `test` and no body; `bindings` is absent on `nums[0] = 9`, whose target names nothing; `extent` is absent whenever measuring the iterable would have meant running player code.

The frame's own top-level fields. `detail` was only half the wire, and the missing half had already been bitten by the same forgotten publish: `1a92eed` added `detail["loop"]` and `frame["types"]` in one commit, and the 1.4.1 on PyPI emits neither. `stage.tsx` reads `frame?.types?.[name]` for the type chip under every variable box, so on the published runner that chip is `undefined` and silently absent — the identical signature as the missing track, and visible in R-50's own before/after screenshots as the `int` labels appearing and disappearing.

So a contract over `detail` keys alone would have declared this defect closed while its second face sat in the evidence. Both halves are declared here, and both are asserted against the installed runner.

The reader's half is the compiler, not a scan: `ComputeLabFrame` in `packages/ui/src/store/gameStore.ts` names these fields, and reading one it does not declare does not compile — the desktop build runs `pnpm --filter ui build`, so CI holds that. `test-frame-contract.mjs` closes the loop by requiring that interface and this declaration to name exactly the same set, which is what makes adding a field to the interface force a release rather than a silent no-op.

`required` is what every frame from `compute_lab_runner` carries. `source` and `location` sit in `optional` because the runner attaches them only when the statement was Located, and `ComputeLabScreen.tsx` agrees — it returns early on `frame.source === undefined`.

`optional` is not the cheap way past the publish. Only `required` is checked against the installed runner, so declaring a new field optional to keep CI quiet also promises the reader handles its absence — and a reader that does not is the defect this file exists to catch, one release later and harder to see. A field the UI draws unconditionally is `required`.

`terminalOnly` is the one field no step frame ever carries. The SDK's `app.py` builds a single closing frame of kind `error` or `limit` from the runner's terminal result, and `error` lives only there. The server already refuses a terminal frame without it (`computeLab.ts`), so it is declared here to be legible to the reader check rather than re-guarded.
